spans.text: This design has significant security implications: if internal tools (such as REPL tools, debugging tools) were included in external builds, even if they were unavailable, they could leak internal architecture information. Dead code elimination eliminates this information leakage risk at the source.
spans.note: The prompt discusses dead code elimination to prevent information leakage and explicitly addresses security implications of internal tools being exposed. It also discusses build security to prevent internal architecture information from leaking to external users.

spans.text: These defaults follow the "fail-closed" principle: security-related methods (such as concurrency safety determination, read-only determination) default to false, and tools must explicitly declare themselves safe to enjoy optimizations like concurrency.
spans.note: The prompt extensively promotes tool safety through multiple mechanisms: fail-closed defaults, three-layer permission checks, concurrency safety marking, sandbox integration, least privilege principles, and hierarchical cancellation signals. It explicitly advocates for validation before execution and safe defaults.

spans.text: **Layer 2: Permission checks (hasPermissionsToUseTool + checkPermissions)**: Contains tool-specific permission logic. Different tools have different permission check granularity -- the Read tool may only check whether a path is in an allow list, while the Bash tool needs to parse commands and assess risk levels.
spans.note: The prompt describes permission systems that keep consequential actions under user control. BashTool requires permission checks, destructive operations trigger stricter permission verification, and the system is designed to confirm with users before executing risky operations. The AskUserQuestionTool exists specifically for user interaction.
